events.title: Up to four reports to three bodies, with two different triggers
events.finding: For one NTN incident a telecom entity reports to CERT-In within six hours of noticing it and to DoT within six hours of becoming aware of it (details within 24 hours). If it also owns designated Critical Telecommunication Infrastructure, it reports within six hours of the incident's occurrence. An access provider whose service is down in a district for more than four hours also files a quality-of-service outage report to TRAI within 24 hours of the outage start (a service-availability report, not a cyber report, but due in the same event). An outage first treated as a fault can pass the occurrence deadline before it is recognised as an attack. (Satellite licensees also report rogue signals and unregistered terminals under Authz Rules 59(4) and 62(7), with no deadline.) No text saying which clock governs, or allowing one joint report, was found in the sources we checked, as of 2026-11-07.

global_examples.quote: without undue delay and in any event within 24 hours of becoming aware of the significant incident, an early warning, which, where applicable, shall indicate whether the significant incident is suspected of being caused by unlawful or malicious acts or could have a cross-border impact
global_examples.shows: One trigger (becoming aware) and one recipient, with staged 24 h / 72 h / one-month reports.

global_examples.instrument: Directive (EU) 2022/2557 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 December 2022 on the resilience of critical entities and repealing Council Directiv
global_examples.quote: Member States shall ensure that, unless operationally unable to do so, critical entities submit an initial notification no later than 24 hours after becoming aware of an incident, followed, where relevant, by a detailed report no later than one month thereafter.
global_examples.shows: Critical entities: one trigger (becoming aware), 24 h initial notification.

global_examples.instrument: 47 CFR Part 4: Disruptions to Communications (Network Outage Reporting System - NORS)
global_examples.quote: All satellite operators shall submit electronically a Notification to the Commission within 120 minutes of discovering that they have experienced on any facilities that they own, operate, lease, or otherwise utilize, of an outage of at least 30 minutes duration that manifests itself as a failure of any of the following key system elements: One or more satellite transponders, satellite beams, inter-satellite links, or entire satellites.
global_examples.shows: Satellite operators report outages to one body, with the clock running from discovery (120 minutes).

recommendation.ask: One trigger ("becoming aware") and one joint portal for NTN incident reports to CERT-In, DoT and TRAI.

interim_action.action: File at the earliest deadline as a precaution; ORCA-NTN drafts each notice and a person sends them.

This is a candidate gap for a human to confirm. Non-binding material exists: IN-SPACEFW-2026-3-2-1, IN-SPACEFW-2026-ANXB-IV, IN-SPACEFW-2026-SDLS, IN-PIB-2026-SPACEFW-ADVISORY.

events.title: No detailed, auditable satellite cyber baseline - one high-level IN-SPACe design line, and the space framework is advisory
events.finding: For licensees under the 2026 Authorisation Rules ("new authorised entities"), binding general security duties apply (TCSR Rule 4; Authz Rule 54 network security and vendor checks, Rule 50 trusted sources, Rule 53 remote-access permission). Their satellite chapter (Authz Rules 59 to 62) adds interception, gateway location, terminal registration, rogue-signal and rogue-terminal reports, and interference monitoring and mitigation on direction (Rule 60(1)(f)). Older GMPCS licensees are bound by licence conditions instead. Satellite-specific cyber controls - protecting command and control links, key management, ground-segment segmentation, telemetry monitoring - appear only in the CERT-In / SIA-India framework, which PIB states is "advisory in nature". India's equipment security standards (NCCS ITSARs, issued under MTCTE) do require a dedicated management interface and secure VPNs - the two entry points of the 2022 KA-SAT attack - but only for office phone exchanges (PABX, ITSAR Group IV 2.12.10, 2.12.12); none of the 64 published ITSARs covers satellite equipment (checked 8 Nov 2026). IN-SPACe's authorisation norms (NGP 2024, which applicants warrant they will follow) contain one satellite-specific line - "Assure cyber security including encryptions at design level and prevent unauthorized commandeering of satellite through adequate data security" (Chapter XI B(v), PDF p. 71) - with no named standard, control list or audit, deviations approved case by case, and nothing on gateways, management networks or user terminals, the parts KA-SAT attacked. No detailed, auditable satellite-specific cyber-resilience baseline (binding controls a regulator can check, covering space, ground and terminal segments) was found in the sources we checked, as of 2026-11-08.

global_examples.quote: Operators of ground-based infrastructure, owned, managed and operated by Member States or by private parties, that support the provision of space-based services, excluding providers of public electronic communications networks
global_examples.shows: Space ground infrastructure is a binding NIS2 sector (ground segment only).

global_examples.quote: business continuity, such as backup management and disaster recovery, and crisis management;
global_examples.shows: So binding NIS2 Art. 21 measures apply to space ground operators.

global_examples.instrument: Regulation (EU) 2021/696 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 28 April 2021 establishing the Union Space Programme and the European Union Agency for
global_examples.quote: the protection of infrastructure, both ground and space, and of the provision of services, particularly against physical or cyber-attacks, including interference with data streams;
global_examples.shows: Binding protection of ground and space infrastructure against cyber-attacks, for EU Space Programme components only.

recommendation.ask: Make a core set of the framework's satellite controls binding, for example as Authz Rule 62 security conditions or a standard notified under Telecom Act s.19.

interim_action.action: Treat framework controls as advice and flag missing ones in every plan; a person decides.

events.title: Feeder-link and inter-satellite-link security is left unspecified, and India has not used its standards power
events.finding: 3GPP TR 33.700-29 says feeder links (gateway to satellite) and inter-satellite links "are not specified in 3GPP" and that generic IP security "can be used". In India, the Telecom Act s.19 lets the government notify telecom security, cyber-security and encryption standards, but no notified standard for satellite links was found in the sources we checked, as of 2026-11-07. The advisory space framework names CCSDS SDLS (see GAP-IN-09). IN-SPACe's NGP 2024 asks satellites for "encryptions at design level" (Chapter XI B(v), PDF p. 71) but names no standard and does not cover feeder or inter-satellite links as such.

global_examples.instrument: Directive (EU) 2022/2555 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 December 2022 on measures for a high common level of cybersecurity across the Union
global_examples.quote: Member States shall ensure that essential and important entities take appropriate and proportionate technical, operational and organisational measures to manage the risks posed to the security of network and information systems which those entities use for their operations or for the provision of their services, and to prevent or minimise the impact of incidents on recipients of their services and on other services.
global_examples.shows: Binding risk-management measures for essential entities, which include space ground infrastructure (NIS2 Annex I).

global_examples.quote: business continuity, such as backup management and disaster recovery, and crisis management;
global_examples.shows: One of the binding minimum measures (business continuity, backup, crisis management).

global_examples.instrument: Regulation (EU) 2019/881 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 17 April 2019 on ENISA (the European Union Agency for Cybersecurity) and on informatio
global_examples.quote: that ICT products, ICT services and ICT processes are secure by default and by design;
global_examples.shows: EU certification framework with secure-by-design objectives and assurance levels (schemes themselves are voluntary unless made mandatory).

recommendation.ask: Notify a satellite-link security standard under s.19 (for example CCSDS SDLS); ask 3GPP and ITU-T to specify feeder-link and inter-satellite-link security.

interim_action.action: Flag satellite links that use no named security standard in every ORCA-NTN plan.

events.explanation: Q-CAP-PWR (Is there a mandatory minimum battery floor?): the only matching record(s) IN-DOT-SOP-2017-3-1-3 do not state whether they bind, so two readings are given and neither is dropped as 'not applicable'.

events.title: Telecom sites must have power redundancy, but no minimum hours are set
events.finding: TRAI requires access providers' quality plans to provide "required redundancies including power", and the DoT SOP asks for "sufficient" battery and fuel backup at vulnerable sites. Neither sets a number of hours. India already sets a 10-hour battery floor for power-grid communication nodes (CEA Reg. 8(11)). No numeric backup floor for telecom sites, including satellite gateways, was found in the sources we checked, as of 2026-11-07.

global_examples.instrument: Decision Adopting Wireless Provider Resiliency Strategies (D.20-07-011)
global_examples.quote: Facilities-based wireless providers shall, in their Communications Resiliency Plan pursuant to Section 6.5.2 of this decision, demonstrate their ability to meet the 72-hour backup power requirement, in Tier 2 and Tier 3 High Fire Threat Districts
global_examples.shows: California: binding 72-hour backup power for wireless facilities in high fire-threat areas.

global_examples.instrument: Decision Adopting Wireline Provider Resiliency Strategies (D.21-02-029)
global_examples.quote: Facilities-based wireline providers shall, in their Communications Resiliency Plan pursuant to Section 5.6.2 of this decision, demonstrate their ability to: (a) meet the 72-hour backup power requirement, in Tier 2 and Tier 3 High Fire Threat Districts
global_examples.shows: California: the same 72-hour floor for wireline facilities.

global_examples.instrument: Improving 911 Reliability; Reliability and Continuity of Communications Networks, Including Broadband Technologies (FCC 13-158)
global_examples.quote: Provisions backup power through fixed generators, portable generators, batteries, fuel cells, or a combination of these or other such sources to maintain full-service functionality, including network monitoring capabilities, for at least 24 hours at full office load or, if the central office hosts a Selective Router, at least 72 hours at full office load; provided, however, that any such portable generators shall be readily available within the time it takes the batteries to drain, notwithstanding potential demand for such generators elsewhere in the service provider’s network.
global_examples.shows: US federal: 911 central offices must provision backup power (certification duty; no hour figure).

recommendation.ask: A minimum backup-power autonomy for sites that carry emergency traffic; India's CEA 10-hour rule for grid communication nodes is a domestic model.

interim_action.action: Shed non-critical load to stretch the battery, using the operator's own threshold.

events.title: Partial gap - no explicit check that the backup path is clean before failover during an attack
events.finding: CTI owners must have disaster-recovery and business-continuity procedures (CTIR Rule 7(1)(i)). Satellite licensees may not fail over to gateways outside India (Authz Rule 60(1)(b)). The advisory space framework asks for failover mechanisms and for integrity checks before resuming operations after an incident. No rule or standard in the sources we checked requires the backup path to be verified uncompromised before traffic is moved during an attack, as of 2026-11-07, although jamming a link to force failover is a known attack path.

global_examples.instrument: Improving 911 Reliability; Reliability and Continuity of Communications Networks, Including Broadband Technologies (FCC 13-158)
global_examples.quote: Eliminated all single points of failure in Critical 911 Circuits or equivalent data paths serving each PSAP.
global_examples.shows: Path diversity for 911 circuits is required, but not an integrity check of the backup path.

global_examples.quote: business continuity, such as backup management and disaster recovery, and crisis management;
global_examples.shows: Business continuity is required, but nothing says a failover path must be checked as clean first.

recommendation.ask: A technical baseline that makes a clean-path check a precondition for failover on NTN backhaul.

interim_action.action: Check the backup path is clean before switching traffic to it, and never to a gateway outside India (Rule 60(1)(b)).

events.verified_by: Charan Velavan, 2026-11-08 - CONFIRMED AS PARTIAL. Continuity duties (CTIR 7(1)(i)) and the advisory secure-restoration line (space framework §7.3, p. 34) partly cover it; the gap is only the missing explicit pre-failover path check.

events.explanation: Q-CAP-PRIO (Is there a legally binding multi-sector capacity priority order?): the only matching record(s) IN-DOT-SOP-2017-3-2-5 do not state whether they bind, so two readings are given and neither is dropped as 'not applicable'.

events.title: Priority callers exist for disaster restoration, but no ranking for sharing scarce backup capacity
events.finding: The DoT disaster SOP names priority callers (emergency operation centres, police, fire, medical, financial institutions and others) for emergency communication and restoration. New licensees must follow government disaster guidelines (Authz Rule 38(1)), which may give the SOP force for them. TRAI asks that voice calls get end-to-end priority on IP interconnection, and Telecom Act s.20(1)(b) lets government order responder messages routed on priority. New licensees must also connect to emergency services and the State disaster platform (Authz Rules 67(1), 71(1)(h)). No standing rule that ranks 112 callers, hospitals, payments and ordinary traffic when satellite backhaul is too small for all of them was found in the sources we checked, as of 2026-11-07.

global_examples.quote: All emergency calls must be treated with the highest priority within the Points of Interconnection.
global_examples.shows: Emergency calls get the highest priority at interconnection (UAE, host country).

global_examples.instrument: Directive (EU) 2018/1972 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 11 December 2018 establishing the European Electronic Communications Code
global_examples.quote: Member States shall ensure that providers of voice communications services take all necessary measures to ensure uninterrupted access to emergency services and uninterrupted transmission of public warnings.
global_examples.shows: Binding duty to keep emergency access and public warnings uninterrupted in a network breakdown.

global_examples.instrument: Constitution of the International Telecommunication Union - Article 40: Priority of Telecommunications Concerning Safety of Life
global_examples.quote: International telecommunication services must give absolute priority to all telecommunications concerning safety of life at sea, on land, in the air or in outer space, as well as to epidemiological telecommunications of exceptional urgency of the World Health Organization.
global_examples.shows: ITU treaty priority for safety-of-life traffic; India is a Member State, but the article covers international services, not domestic capacity allocation.

recommendation.ask: Turn the SOP priority callers into a standing, ordered list for scarce backup capacity, including satellite backhaul.

interim_action.action: Share the remaining capacity using the SOP priority callers with 112 first, then switch traffic to the backup link; a person approves.

events.title: No binding duty for a satellite operator to warn the services that depend on it
events.finding: Reports flow to CERT-In, DoT and TRAI. CERT-In's statutory role includes disseminating incident information and alerts, and the government may tell the public or require the operator to do so (TCSR Rule 7(2)). New authorised entities may not share network information with others without prior written government approval (Authz Rule 37(5)). The text on an operator warning its dependants is in the advisory space framework (Annexure B item 4.2; coordination in §6.5 and §9.2), with no deadline. No binding duty for a satellite operator to warn the mobile operators, utilities, hospitals or banks that use its ground network was found in the sources we checked, as of 2026-11-07.

global_examples.quote: Where appropriate, entities concerned shall notify, without undue delay, the recipients of their services of significant incidents that are likely to adversely affect the provision of those services.
global_examples.shows: Binding duty to notify the recipients of services of significant incidents.

global_examples.quote: essential and important entities communicate, without undue delay, to the recipients of their services that are potentially affected by a significant cyber threat any measures or remedies that those recipients are able to take in response to that threat
global_examples.shows: Binding duty to tell affected recipients about measures they can take against a significant cyber threat.

recommendation.ask: A binding duty, with a deadline, for NTN operators to warn the services that depend on them, with a standing Rule 37(5) approval for such warnings; compare NIS2 Art. 23(1) and 23(2).

interim_action.action: Send a human-approved warning to the dependent services, after checking whether Rule 37(5) approval is needed.
